title: Year two close: the book in your hands
hook: a library you've walked through, from the garden to the shore at breakfast

segments.voice: Yesterday, Christmas and the Word made flesh, and your line was he dwelt among us. Where did you find the holy in something ordinary? Day six hundred ninety-six.

This year began in a garden, where God walked in the cool of the day. Then came a desert crossed by a whole people. A room full of songs, some joyful, some furious. Prophets shouting in the street. Then Luke and John, all the way to a charcoal fire on a beach at dawn where, in John's telling, the risen Jesus cooked breakfast for his friends. And lately, a few letters left on the table. Today is the last day of year two. Before it closes, one look back, and one verse to take with you.
screen: `A GARDEN, A DESERT, A ROOM OF SONGS.`

segments.voice: Year two had seven parts. Genesis: beginnings, a garden, a flood, a family that kept going wrong and kept being carried. Exodus: slaves, a sea, manna, a mountain, a golden calf, and long years in the wilderness. The Psalms and the wisdom books: prayers for every mood, and wisdom that knows life is short and good. The prophets: a burning coal, a potter, dry bones, a sulking prophet, a king on a donkey. Luke, read through: outsiders, meals and mercy. John, read through: the Word, the signs, the bread and the light and the good shepherd, and that breakfast on the shore. And three letters of joy, faith and love: Philippians, James and First John, with the elder's two short notes. Now the verse for today. Near the end of Deuteronomy, Moses gives his last speeches before the people cross into the land without him. He tells them the commandment isn't hidden away. It isn't up in heaven, where someone would have to climb and fetch it. It isn't across the sea, where someone would have to sail out and bring it back. In the King James Bible: "But the word is very nigh unto thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart, that thou mayest do it." Very nigh. Near. The Hebrew word is karov: close by, within reach. Centuries later, Paul quoted this same line in his letter to the Romans: "The word is nigh thee, even in thy mouth, and in thy heart." The verse is read in Jewish and Christian tradition, each in its own way. But the picture is shared: the word isn't a far-off mountain only experts can climb. It's meant to be near enough to say, and to keep. After a year of reading, the book itself is in your hands.
screen: `NOT IN HEAVEN, NOT ACROSS THE SEA.`
then, large: `THE WORD IS VERY NIGH UNTO THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write the one verse you'll keep. Settle, and breathe. Let the year go past: the garden, the desert, the songs, the prophets, the roads of Luke, the shore in John, the letters. Which verse stayed? Maybe the Lord is my shepherd. Maybe a line from a prophet, or no fear in love, or something small nobody else would pick. Don't choose the most famous one. Choose the one that's already near you, the one you catch yourself saying. After the bell, write it down by hand. If you pray, you can give thanks for a year of reading. The bell holds the time.
Karov. Hebrew for near, close by: the word Moses said wasn't far off in heaven or across the sea, but near enough to say, and to keep.

Your line: the word is near you. Today, put your verse where your hand will find it: a pocket, a wallet, a phone case. Tomorrow, year three begins with Joshua and the long story of Israel. Day six hundred ninety-six.

howItsDone: Some Christians keep a favorite verse close, memorized, written in a Bible's margin or posted at home, and churches sometimes mark the end of a season of reading with a time of looking back and giving thanks.
